title: Advisory Locks
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Advisory Locks.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to transaction-level advisory locks.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Advisory Locks. Its primary job is to help you keep multi-step changes atomic and reason about snapshots, locks, waits, retries and competing transactions. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing advisory locks teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: keep multi-step changes atomic and reason about snapshots, locks, waits, retries and competing transactions. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: Transaction-level advisory locks
items.text: Mark the transaction boundary explicitly and verify both the commit path and a rollback path in a disposable database.

items.text: Identify the rows and transaction snapshots involved; test a second session and document blocking or retry behavior.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Advisory Locks
content_blocks.expected_output: Shows locks held or awaited by the current backend, subject to visibility and query context.
content_blocks.safety_note: Do not deliberately create production blocking or deadlocks for a lesson.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run with monitoring permissions in a development database.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Advisory Locks”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Transaction-level advisory locks”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Transaction-level advisory locks”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Advisory Locks, with an explanation of “Transaction-level advisory locks”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Advisory Locks fits into the broader goal to keep multi-step changes atomic and reason about snapshots, locks, waits, retries and competing transactions.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Transaction-level advisory locks, Session-level advisory locks, Application-defined locking.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
